nameStory: Hart's Jumping Spider is named after Charles Frederick Hart, a 19th-century naturalist who made significant contributions to North American spider taxonomy. Like many scientific names that honor researchers, this spider carries forward the legacy of someone who dedicated their life to understanding the intricate world of arachnids.
description: Hart's Jumping Spider is a small, compact member of the jumping spider family, known for their excellent vision and hunting prowess. These tiny predators typically measure just a few millimeters in body length, with sturdy, somewhat chunky proportions typical of jumping spiders. Like all jumping spiders, they have large, forward-facing eyes that give them an almost curious, intelligent expression. Their coloration tends to be subtle browns and grays that help them blend into bark and leaf litter.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a distinctive pattern, with the middle pair being especially prominent and giving the spider an alert, almost puppy-like appearance

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, robust build with a relatively short, stocky abdomen and thick, powerful front legs that feel sturdy when gently observed

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Actively hunts by stalking prey with jerky, deliberate movements, often turning to watch you with curious head tilts when approached

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider measuring just a few millimeters in body length, easily fitting on a fingernail with room to spare

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Does not build webs for catching prey, but creates small silk retreats under bark or stones that feel like tiny, dense silk pouches

habitat: Hart's Jumping Spider can be found in various woodland habitats throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with plenty of bark crevices and leaf litter. Look for them on tree trunks, fallen logs, and rocky outcrops where they hunt for small insects and other tiny prey. They seem to prefer slightly drier microhabitats compared to some other jumping spiders.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter retreats to begin hunting and mating activities.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily observed hunting during daylight hours and females may be found guarding egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues but begins to slow as spiders prepare winter retreats, with late-season mating still possible.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in silk-lined retreats under bark, stones, or in leaf litter, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Jumping spiders like Hart's have vision that's so acute they can see details and movement up to 20 times their body length away - imagine being able to clearly see someone's facial expressions from over 100 feet away!
confusionNotes: Hart's Jumping Spider can be confused with other small jumping spiders in the Tutelina genus, but the specific eye arrangement and body proportions help distinguish it. Remember: all jumping spiders share those distinctive large front eyes, but Hart's has a particularly compact, robust build compared to more elongated species.
compareHints: Hart's Jumping Spider differs from its close relatives like the Thin-spined Jumping Spider by having a more robust, stocky build rather than an elongated appearance. Compared to the Thick-spined Jumping Spider, Hart's tends to have subtler coloration and slightly different proportions in the eye arrangement. Within the jumping spider family overall, Tutelina species are generally smaller and more conservatively colored than the flashier, more colorful jumping spiders many people are familiar with.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tutelina relatives in New England, the Thin-spined Jumping Spider is distinguished by its delicate leg spines compared to the robust spines of the Thick-spined Jumping Spider.
The Thick-spined Jumping Spider differs from Hart's Jumping Spider and the Thin-spined Jumping Spider primarily in the robustness of its leg spines - they're noticeably thicker and more substantial.
Distinguishing between Tutelina species requires very close examination and is challenging even for experts.
